title: Does Banning Social Media for Teens Actually Work?

content:
Australia's ban on social media for anyone under 16 kicked in on December 10, 2025, making it the world's first national law of its kind. Nine months in, the honest answer is: it hasn't worked as promised. Over 85% of Australian teens are still on major platforms. Early research from The BMJ found no measurable drop in social media use. And now India's watching, deciding whether to follow. Here's what the data actually shows.

Key Takeaways

  • Australia's ban launched in December 2025; three months later, over 85% of under-16s were still using major platforms.
  • An early BMJ analysis found no measurable reduction in social media use after the ban.
  • Nearly 75% of Australian 14- to 15-year-olds didn't comply, mainly because they felt their peers weren't either.
  • India has 250+ million internet users under 18, making enforcement far harder than it was in Australia.
  • Evidence supports reducing screen time as more effective than outright blocking access.

What Did Australia's Ban Actually Do?

The law was straightforward on paper. Starting December 2025, platforms like Instagram, TikTok, and Snapchat were required to prevent users under 16 from holding accounts. Non-compliance meant fines up to A$54.6 million, roughly 330 crore rupees. Sounds decisive. The reality turned out to be messier.

Three months after the ban, surveys showed that more than 85% of under-16s were still active on at least one major platform. An August 2026 analysis found little evidence that Australia's restrictions had led to any short-term reduction in use. Teens faked their birth year or borrowed a parent's account. The workarounds were simple enough, and plenty of them figured this out quickly.

That's not entirely Australia's fault. Age verification online is genuinely hard. Platforms check a birth year at signup, and a determined 15-year-old can type the wrong one in about three seconds. Building real verification through government ID or biometrics raises its own privacy questions, and no country has solved this cleanly yet.

Why Did 75% of Australian Teens Ignore the Ban?

This is the part most news articles skip. Research found that nearly 75% of 14- to 15-year-olds weren't complying, and the main reason was social pressure. They percieved that their peers weren't following the ban either, so staying off felt pointless. The social pull of these platforms is exactly what makes banning them hard: if everyone else is still on Instagram, leaving feels like punishment, not protection.

Bans work when enforcement is visible and the banned thing is easy to intercept. Social media lives on a phone in a pocket. Without device-level controls or meaningful parental involvement, platform-level bans are definately going to stay porous. Australia learned this the hard way, and it's a lesson worth studying before India writes its own version.

Australia vs India: The Comparison That Matters

The scale gap is the real issue. India has more under-18 internet users than Australia has people. Any enforcement system that struggles in a relatively small, high-income country would face a fundamentally different challenge in India, where cheap smartphones and free mobile data connected hundreds of millions of children in under a decade.

Does the Science Say Banning Social Media Helps Teen Mental Health?

Honestly, the evidence is thin. A review published in mid-2026 found no clear short-term mental health improvements from Australia's ban. That doesn't mean the policy has no long-term value. Behavior change takes time to show up in population-level health data. But the early numbers aren't inspiring.

What does have solid evidence: reducing screen time by even one hour a day, consistently, shows measurable improvements in sleep and anxiety. A 2025 meta-analysis of 20 randomized controlled trials found that cutting social media use had a meaningful effect on self-esteem, loneliness, and life satisfaction. The key word is "reducing," not "removing." Complete bans may not produce better outcomes than structured limits.

This matters for India. The Economic Survey 2026 recommended screen-time limits and phone-free school zones rather than outright platform bans. That approach has more research support than a blanket age restriction does, and it's a seperate question from whether a ban is politically satisfying.

Should India Ban Social Media for Under-16s?

PM Modi praised Australia's approach at the Australia-India Annual Leaders' Summit in July 2026. Karnataka has moved to consider restrictions. Andhra Pradesh and Goa are studying similar rules.

The political logic is clear. Parents are worried. Schools are overwhelmed. The Economic Survey calling digital addiction a national concern shows this has moved beyond parental anxiety into policy territory. And something genuinely needs to happen.

But copying Australia's model without better enforcement tools would likely produce similar results: a law that exists, teens who mostly bypass it, and a gap between the policy and the actual problem. What works, based on current evidence: parental controls built into devices and school-day phone restrictions with real consequences, plus platforms required to default to conservative settings for accounts claiming to be under 18.

A ban could still be part of the picture, particularly if paired with proper age verification. But bans alone, without device-level or family-level reinforcement, haven't shown they can hold. India would be starting with much larger numbers, fewer enforcement resources per user, and a culture of cheap, freely available devices that makes removal harder to enforce than in almost any country Australia compared itself to.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Australia's social media ban for under-16s actually work?

Not yet, based on early data. Three months after it launched in December 2025, over 85% of Australian teens were still using major platforms. An early BMJ analysis found no measurable reduction in social media use. Long-term outcomes may differ, but short-term compliance has been low.

Is India going to ban social media for kids under 16?

India is actively considering it. PM Modi praised Australia's ban in July 2026, and states including Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Goa are studying similar restrictions. The Economic Survey 2026 flagged digital addiction as a national concern, but no central law has been passed yet.

Why did Australian teens still use social media after the ban?

Mainly social pressure. Nearly 75% of 14- to 15-year-olds felt their peers weren't complying either, so opting out felt pointless. Age verification is also easy to bypass by entering a false birth year. Without device-level controls, platform-only restrictions stay porous.

What actually reduces teens' social media use?

Research supports reducing time rather than removing access entirely. Cutting daily use by one hour shows measurable improvements in sleep and anxiety. Parental controls, phone-free school policies, and platform defaults that limit session time have more evidence behind them than outright bans for teens.

How many Indian children use the internet?

India has over 250 million internet users under 18. That's more than Australia's total population. This makes India's enforcement challenge significantly larger than what Australia faced, and it's a key reason a direct policy copy may not produce comparable results.

The Short Version

Australia's ban is a live, real-world test, and the early data is honest: blocking social media for teens is harder than it looks, and most find workarounds. Mental health benefits haven't shown up yet in the data. India should watch closely, but replicating the model without better enforcement tools would likely produce the same gaps. Reducing time, not blocking access entirely, is what the evidence actually backs right now.
